sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celts did not build temples as the Romans did. They met to worship in the open air. Their sacred places were nemetons, or sacred woods, where offerings were made. They also gathered on hilltops such as Uisneach and Tara. There the great fires burned on festival days. They met at holy wells too, where inauguration rites were held. Some stone buildings survive that scholars call temples or castles. At the British site of Maiden Castle in Dorset, a circular building was found. It dates to the first century BCE. The circle held cosmological meaning for the Celts. So the building is read as religious. Similar round structures stood at Emain Macha and Dun Ailinne in Ireland. A central post at Emain Macha may mark the sacred tree in a grove.

okr.objective: Record how the Celts practiced worship without temples.
